analysis.tldr: If the government struggles to control its spending, it may have to borrow more, which can push up overall interest rates in the economy.
the_story: Deutsche Bank projects India's fiscal deficit (the gap between government spending and earnings) for the financial year 2028 will stay at 4.3% of GDP (Gross Domestic Product, the total value of goods and services produced).
The report highlights that efforts to bring down this deficit face challenges because of rising government expenditure and subsidy bills.
Economic growth is expected to remain steady, with GDP growth forecast at 7.3% for FY27 and 7.2% for FY28.
Retail inflation (the rate at which everyday prices rise for consumers) has surpassed the RBI's (Reserve Bank of India, the central bank) upper threshold, driven primarily by higher food prices.
analysis.what_happened: Deutsche Bank released a report stating that India's fiscal deficit for FY28 will remain at 4.3% of GDP. This projection is driven by challenges in cutting government spending and high subsidy bills, even as overall economic growth and inflation remain key economic factors.
analysis.analogy: It is like a household running a monthly budget where expenses and grocery bills keep creeping up, making it harder to save extra money, forcing the family to rely more on credit cards.
why_it_matters_india: Higher government spending and subsidies keep the fiscal deficit at 4.3% of GDP for FY28.
To cover this gap, the government needs to borrow money from the market.
When the government borrows heavily, it increases competition for funds, which can keep bond yields (the interest rate the government pays to borrow) elevated.
Higher yields across the economy can eventually make loans like home and car loans costlier for everyday people.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: High government borrowing requirements can push yields up, which generally means costlier loans for everyone — bad for borrowers.
The article notes that retail inflation has already surpassed the central bank's upper limit due to food prices, making household budgets tighter.
Persistent inflation and high borrowing costs can weigh down corporate profit margins, which is usually a negative sign for stock markets.

watch_next: Upcoming government budget announcements for spending and subsidy targets
RBI updates on retail inflation and interest rate decisions
analysis.caveats: Only the headline and a short wire text summary were available, meaning detailed sectoral impacts are based on general economic logic rather than full report data.

analysis.tldr: Indian bond markets are holding back and staying nervous because people expect interest rates to go up soon, which usually makes borrowing costs more expensive for everyone.
the_story: The bond market (where governments and companies borrow money by selling fixed-income papers) is staying cautious because of ongoing inflation (rising prices) and expected interest rate hikes.
Analysts from Equirus predict the RBI (Reserve Bank of India, the country's central bank) will raise its key interest rate by 25 basis points (0.25 percentage points) in its upcoming review.
Market yields (the actual returns investors get on bonds) will also be pushed and pulled by global tensions and bond movements around the world.
On the bright side, money coming in from FIIs (Foreign Portfolio Investors, big overseas funds) and a stable currency (rupee) might help support bond yields.
analysis.what_happened: The bond market is acting nervous and guarded ahead of the RBI's policy meeting. This caution is caused by stubborn inflation and predictions that the central bank will raise interest rates to cool things down.
analysis.analogy: It is like a group of people waiting outside a shop because they heard the store owner is about to raise prices — nobody wants to buy just yet until they see how much more expensive things get.
why_it_matters_india: Inflation stays persistent and the RBI looks at it -> The central bank considers raising interest rates (the cost of borrowing money) -> Market yields (the return demanded by bond investors) tend to rise.
When bond yields rise, it becomes more expensive for the government and companies to borrow money -> This can eventually push up loan costs for ordinary people.
At the same time, money coming in from foreign investors (FIIs) acts like a cushion, helping keep the currency and bond market stable.
Global events and overseas bond movements also spill over, keeping local bond traders on edge.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (the interest rate the government pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: As analysts predict rate hikes and cautious trading, yields go up — which generally means borrowing costs get dearer for the economy, making it tough for borrowers.

impacts.target: Banking stocks like SBI, Axis Bank, and HDFC Bank
impacts.rationale: Cautious bond markets and rising yields can squeeze bank portfolios, which is usually a short-term headache for bank stock investors.
Stable currency conditions and foreign portfolio inflows provide support, keeping the rupee steady, which is good for keeping imported goods like oil from getting suddenly pricier.

watch_next: The official RBI monetary policy announcement and its actual decision on interest rates
Updates on foreign portfolio investor (FII) money inflows into India
analysis.caveats: If the RBI surprises the market by keeping interest rates unchanged instead of hiking them, bond yields could quickly drop back down.

events.headline: Shrinkflation and the constraints of monetary tightening

items.title: Shrinkflation and the constraints of monetary tightening
items.summary: The RBI’s 25-basis-point repo rate hike is aimed at cost-push inflation. How producers respond to rising prices determines whether it works.

events.article_text:
Published : Nov 19, 2026 14:16 IST - 5 MINS READ

A pedestrian walks past the entrance of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) headquarters in Mumbai on October 7, 2026. India's central bank hiked interest rates for the first time in more than three years on October 7, as the Middle East conflict stokes inflation in Asia's third-largest economy and batters a weakened rupee. | Photo Credit: PUNIT PARANJPE/AFP

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) raised the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent on October 7, 2026, its first increase since February 2023. The aim is to bring down cost-push inflation, driven by higher energy prices after the conflict in West Asia.

According to conventional economic theory, a central bank can reduce the demand for credit by raising interest rates, which slows the rise in prices. Cost-push inflation complicates this, because higher rates reduce both corporate and consumer demand.

The cost is not only higher equated monthly instalments (EMIs). Jobs are also lost or never created.

Policymakers therefore need to know how producers react to inflation. The market and the state respond differently, and each can learn from the other.

This article looks at three market responses to inflation and how public policy responds to each. They are shrinkflation, skimpflation, and expandingstatic, the article’s term for offering more of a product at an unchanged price.

Shrinkflation is a hidden price increase: manufacturers reduce a product’s weight, size, or quantity and keep the price the same. In 2022, Hindustan Unilever’s Rs.10 Vim bar went from 155 g to 135 g, and a Haldiram’s aloo bhujia pack at the same price went from 55 g to 42 g.

Consumers pay the same for less and must buy more often. Their purchasing power falls, and the extra spending adds to inflation.

The evidence on scale is mixed. In 2017, the UK’s Office for National Statistics found that shrinking packs had no effect on overall inflation, though they raised the prices of chocolates and sweets.

Shrinkflation does not stop price increases. It hides them, and inflation stays high long after the original causes have gone.

Once prices settle at a higher level, they stay there. Producers then move to expandingstatic: they increase a product’s quantity or size, or bundle accessories with it, at prevailing prices.

Customers get more for the same money and buy less often, so spending falls. With prices high enough to reward output, the law of supply applies: rising prices encourage rising production.

Skimpflation is the practice of lowering the quality of a product or service while keeping the price unchanged. Producers use cheaper ingredients, cut staff, cut service features, or offer fewer amenities.

In a wealthy society, where consumers are sensitive to quality, poor products and services discourage repeat purchases. In a poor society, skimpflation persists and has effects similar to those of shrinkflation.

Laws and regulation limit the practice, as does business ethics. How far skimpflation succeeds depends on the relationship between political economy and society, and that relationship limits how long the market can use it.

When a central bank raises the repo rate during shrinkflation, it asks consumers to spend less, although they already have to buy more often to get the same quantity. Policy and social reality conflict.

Households facing shrinkflation and higher borrowing costs spend less on industrial goods and more on essentials, and their standard of living falls. Fiscal policy can respond with tax cuts, higher public spending, or both, to raise demand for industrial goods, production, and living standards.

Manufacturers, however, have little reason to raise production during shrinkflation. They have raised effective prices, sell fewer industrial goods, and earn higher mark-ups.

Monetary tightening therefore fails to bring inflation down during shrinkflation. It also adds to household distress and makes fiscal policy less effective.

Expandingstatic works differently. It stabilises prices at a higher level, and with more product on offer at the same price, spending falls.

Stable prices allow the central bank to cut the repo rate, which raises industrial output. Producers can also use the reserve capacity they built up from the mark-ups they earned during shrinkflation.

At this stage the government can raise public spending and the central bank can ease monetary policy, and producers are likely to increase output. A larger state can also crowd in private producers through positive externalities, although many economists warn that heavy government borrowing can crowd out private investment by raising interest rates.

These conditions encourage investment in alternative production methods and goods that reduce the effects of cost-push inflation. Rising fuel prices, for instance, have contributed to higher manufacture and sale of electric vehicles.

Because law and business ethics keep skimpflation in check, it does not bring the market into conflict with state policy. Shrinkflation does.

During shrinkflation, consumers must spend more while the central bank wants them to spend less, and producers cut quantity while fiscal policy tries to raise consumption. Producers, consumers, and public policy work at cross-purposes.

Public policy is more likely to succeed during expandingstatic, when producers and policymakers both want more output. Rising output brings more jobs, in line with the Phillips curve, which posits a short-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment.

Whether the RBI’s October hike works depends on which of the two applies. If producers keep shrinking packs, tightening alone will not bring down cost-push inflation, and public policy must work to reduce shrinkflation and speed up expandingstatic.

Ajay Kumar Mishra teaches Economics at Lalit Narayan Mithila University, Darbhanga, Bihar. He has obtained his PhD from the Centre for South Asian Studies, JNU, New Delhi.

analysis.tldr: When the Reserve Bank of India raises interest rates while companies secretly shrink product sizes, your loan EMIs get costlier without actually stopping inflation.
the_story: On October 7, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) raised its policy repo rate (the interest rate the central bank charges commercial banks) by 25 basis points (0.25 percentage points) to 5.50 per cent, its first hike since February 2023.
The hike aims to fight cost-push inflation (rising prices driven by higher production costs) caused by surging energy prices from the West Asian conflict.

To cope with price pressures without raising stated prices, companies use shrinkflation (reducing a product's size or weight at the same price, like Hindustan Unilever's Vim bar dropping from 155g to 135g in 2022).
Monetary tightening (raising interest rates to cool the economy) conflicts with shrinkflation because households are already forced to spend more to buy smaller quantities more often.
The article contrasts shrinkflation with expandingstatic (offering more product at an unchanged price) and skimpflation (lowering product quality at the same price).
analysis.what_happened: The Reserve Bank of India raised its key interest rate to 5.50 per cent to combat inflation sparked by higher energy costs from West Asia. However, because companies are practicing shrinkflation—giving less product for the same money—households must spend extra just to buy basics, making the central bank's rate hikes less effective at lowering prices.
analysis.analogy: It is like a gym increasing your membership fee to stop you from eating junk food, while the snack shop secretly halves the size of your protein bar so you have to buy two anyway.
why_it_matters_india: The RBI raises the policy repo rate -> Commercial banks pass on higher costs, making home, auto, and business loans more expensive.
Higher repo rate -> Equated monthly instalments (EMIs) increase for households, raising their financial burden.
Shrinkflation forces consumers to spend more on everyday essentials -> Households have less money left to spend on industrial goods, slowing down business growth.
Monetary tightening collides with shrinkflation -> Higher interest rates fail to lower inflation while damaging household standards of living and job creation.

impacts.rationale: higher repo rates mean banks raise borrowing costs, which is bad for ordinary loan borrowers as monthly payments increase.
shrinkflation and high energy costs keep inflation sticky despite central bank rate hikes, which hurts everyday purchasing power.
buying smaller pack sizes for the same price means consumers get less for their money, lowering living standards.

watch_next: Whether the RBI introduces further interest rate hikes in upcoming monetary policy meetings
Shifts in how consumer goods manufacturers adjust package sizes or pricing strategies
analysis.caveats: If manufacturers quickly transition from shrinkflation to expandingstatic by offering more value, central policy tools could regain their effectiveness in lowering prices.

events.headline: Members briefed on food export restrictions history, safeguard mechanism

items.title: Members briefed on food export restrictions history, safeguard mechanism
items.summary: The history of negotiations on export restrictions on food and a proposed special safeguard mechanism (SSM) for developing economies were the focus of meetings of the Committee on Agriculture's negotiations body on 23 November. This was the latest in a series of thematic briefings by the WTO Secretariat, as members explore options for a path forward in the stalled negotiations on agricultural trade.

events.article_text:
This note has been prepared by the WTO Secretariat to assist public understanding about the work of the WTO's councils, committees and other bodies. It is not intended as a complete account of all issues raised at the meeting. These can be found in the formal meeting minutes.

At a meeting of the Committee on Agriculture in Special Session (CoA-SS), WTO Secretariat staff delivered two presentations, at the request of members. The first concerned the history of WTO negotiations regarding export restrictions on food, while the second looked at a proposed SSM - a mechanism that would allow developing economies to raise tariffs temporarily in the event of a sudden surge in the volume of imports or of a fall in prices. The presentations are part of a series looking at how talks on various negotiating topics were negotiated and have evolved over time.

During the meeting, the Chair, Ambassador Ali Sarfraz Hussain (Pakistan), said that the sessions were designed to provide a common factual basis for members' exchanges, and that they complemented other initiatives aimed at promoting evidence-based negotiations. He asked members to reflect on their positions and share their candid views on how to advance the negotiations.

Negotiations on agriculture began in 2000, under Article 20 of the Agreement on Agriculture, but have achieved only limited progress since then. (See WTO briefing note online here.)

Trade officials participating in the meeting expressed appreciation to WTO Secretariat staff for the briefings. Several said that they found the presentations to be highly informative, and that they had helped to deepen their understanding of why and how negotiating proposals and decisions had been made during past talks.

Several delegations stressed the importance of open, predictable and transparent agricultural trade and highlighted the adverse effects that export restrictions could have on food security, especially for least-developed countries (LDCs) and net food-importing developing countries (NFIDCs). They emphasized the importance of enhancing the transparency and predictability of export restrictions by clarifying and strengthening existing disciplines.

Other delegations stressed the importance of preserving policy space for the use of export restrictions when addressing food security challenges in developing economies. They said that they considered that the existing disciplines strike a generally appropriate balance, and that efforts should focus on the effective implementation of existing rules.

Many delegations took the floor to state their positions on the SSM, asserting that it was a vital tool for protecting farmers' livelihoods in developing economies. Several stated that trade ministers had instructed WTO members to pursue negotiations on the SSM at ministerial conferences, and that work should proceed swiftly and on a dedicated track to find a durable solution.

Some agricultural exporting members again expressed the view that progress on this topic could not be made in isolation from broader agricultural market access reform negotiations, with one member calling for members to first reconcile the fundamental difference regarding the question of linkage between food export restrictions and the SSM.

Two events forming part of the Dialogue on Emerging Agricultural Trade Issues (EAT) were announced during the CoA-SS meeting. One event, organized by Switzerland and Thailand, on the transition to sustainable agriculture, took place on 23 November. The other, organized by China and Brazil, on the topic of farmers, cooperatives and trade, took place on 24 November. A side event on export restrictions, with invited experts from international organizations and the private sector, was organized by Japan on 25 November.

Several delegations expressed the view that the WTO Secretariat's historical presentations, together with the EAT Issues initiatives, should constitute a foundation for follow-up technical discussions and evidence-based engagement.

The afternoon session included a discussion on the procurement of food at administered prices for public stocks in developing economies. The Chair noted that there had been no new submissions on public food stockholding since the thematic session held during the 27 October meeting.

Several members again suggested that talks should proceed on the basis of a joint WTO proposal submitted over four years ago by roughly 80 developing WTO members spanning the African group, the African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) Group and the G-33 group of developing economies. The proposal calls for a revision of the WTO methodology for calculating support associated with the purchase of food at administered prices for public stocks in developing countries.

Some members spoke in favour of new approaches to the talks, while several proponents said that talks in this area should proceed in line with previous ministerial mandates. At least one member said that it would not support moves toward a standalone outcome on public stockholding if this issue is not included in a more comprehensive deal, given that this issue concerns market price support.

The Chair concluded by emphasizing that, while the presentations had provided valuable historical context, it was ultimately for members to engage with one another and take the negotiations forward. He urged them to use the upcoming weeks and the holiday period to reflect on possible avenues for progress. The Chair will continue to consult with members with a view to facilitating convergence on a shared path forward.

The next meeting of the CoA-SS is planned for 25 January. On this occasion, the WTO Secretariat will deliver the last presentation in its series on the history of the agriculture negotiations, focusing on cotton.

analysis.tldr: Global trade talks on farm rules and food security could eventually sway what India pays for imports and how it supports its local farmers, though no actual law changes happened yet.
the_story: At a World Trade Organization (WTO) Committee on Agriculture meeting, staff delivered presentations on the history of food export restrictions and a proposed safeguard mechanism (SSM).
The SSM would let developing economies temporarily raise import taxes if they face a sudden flood of imports or falling prices.
Delegations debated whether export restrictions hurt food security for poorer countries, or if developing nations need them as policy space.
Members also discussed public food stockholding—buying food at administered prices—and whether to update the calculation rules proposed years ago by around 80 developing nations.
analysis.what_happened: Officials at the World Trade Organization met to review the history of agricultural trade negotiations, food export restrictions, and special safeguards for developing countries. Because these talks have dragged on slowly since 2000 with limited progress, the meeting aimed to build a shared factual history to help countries eventually break the deadlock.
analysis.analogy: It is like a group of business partners opening up their old meeting minutes from twenty years ago to figure out why they can never agree on a discount policy for raw materials.
why_it_matters_india: WTO meetings discuss rules around public food stockholding, which directly touches how developing nations buy food from farmers at fixed prices.
India is a major player in agricultural trade and relies on policies to protect local farmers and maintain public food stocks.
Any future global agreement on export restrictions or import taxes (tariffs) could affect India's ability to restrict or promote food exports depending on domestic food security.
However, since this meeting was only a historical briefing with no final decisions made, there is no immediate change to Indian markets or policies.

impacts.rationale: Only a long-term global trade deal affecting food supplies could alter food inflation; right now, these talks have no direct impact on prices.
A WTO administrative briefing does not sway broader corporate earnings or market sentiment for major Indian stocks.

watch_next: The next WTO Committee on Agriculture meeting scheduled for 25 January
Any formal proposals regarding public food stockholding or special safeguard mechanisms
analysis.caveats: These discussions are strictly exploratory and historical, meaning they may not translate into binding global rules anytime soon.

events.headline: Oil Surge Pushes Indonesia to Mull First Subsidized Fuel Price Hike in Years

items.title: Oil Surge Pushes Indonesia to Mull First Subsidized Fuel Price Hike in Years
items.summary: Indonesia, the largest economy in Southeast Asia, has discussed hiking the price of subsidized fuel for the first time since 2022, as the weakening local currency and persistently high oil prices weigh on government outlays for funding the subsidies. Indonesia, the world’s fourth-most populous country, hasn’t removed or reduced subsidies for gasoline and fuel amid the Strait of Hormuz crisis. The country, a net oil importer despite having domestic oil production, has subsidized fuel in one form or another since it gained independence…

events.article_text:
OPEC+ Faces Growing Pressure As Iraq Pushes for Higher Quota

Indonesia, the largest economy in Southeast Asia, has discussed hiking the price of subsidized fuel for the first time since 2022, as the weakening local currency and persistently high oil prices weigh on government outlays for funding the subsidies.

Indonesia, the world’s fourth-most populous country, hasn’t removed or reduced subsidies for gasoline and fuel amid the Strait of Hormuz crisis. The country, a net oil importer despite having domestic oil production, has subsidized fuel in one form or another since it gained independence in the 1940s.

This year, the spike in oil prices has significantly raised the government’s spending on subsidizing fuels and keeping them well below market rates. Currently, gasoline and diesel are being sold in Indonesia at about half and less than a third, respectively, of their fair-value price.

As a result, Indonesia’s budget has been strained, its currency, the Indonesian rupiah, has crashed to an all-time low against the U.S. dollar, and the stock market tumbled amid loss of investor confidence.

Indonesia is now reportedly considering hiking the price of subsidized fuel in early 2027, in what would be the first such move since 2022, state officials and industry sources told Reuters on Friday.

Indonesia last week held a meeting to discuss a potential price hike for subsidized fuels. The meeting included representatives of the economy ministry, state energy giant Pertamina, and Bank of Indonesia, the central bank, according to Reuters’ sources.

However, no decision on whether to hike fuel prices has been reached at the meeting. The size of a potential increase hasn’t been discussed, either, the sources told the publication.

Due to the spike in international crude oil prices, Indonesia’s government will have to spend as much as $27.2 billion (500 trillion Indonesian rupiah) on fuel subsidies this year alone. The sum would be 30% higher than the original estimate for subsidies before the Iran war hit oil supplies and hiked international oil and fuel prices.

analysis.tldr: Rising global oil prices are putting heavy pressure on oil-importing countries like Indonesia, which serves as a warning sign for higher imported energy costs in India.
the_story: Indonesia is discussing raising its subsidized fuel prices for the first time since 2022 because of high global oil prices and a weakening local currency.
The spike in oil prices is expected to cost Indonesia $27.2 billion (500 trillion Indonesian rupiah) on fuel subsidies this year, which is 30% higher than originally estimated.
Gasoline and diesel in Indonesia are currently sold at about half and less than a third of their fair-value prices, straining the government budget.

Representatives from the economy ministry, state energy giant Pertamina, and Bank of Indonesia held a meeting last week to discuss a potential price hike for early 2027, though no final decision has been made yet.
analysis.what_happened: Global crude oil prices have surged due to supply issues like the Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz crisis. This has made imported fuel extremely expensive for countries that buy oil from abroad, forcing governments like Indonesia to spend billions more on keeping fuel cheap for citizens.
analysis.analogy: It is like running a community kitchen where you promised to sell meals at a fixed low price, but suddenly the cost of vegetables triples—forcing you to either go bankrupt or finally charge people more.
why_it_matters_india: Global oil prices surge due to Middle East supply disruptions -> India, which imports most of its oil, faces higher crude import bills.
Higher import bills mean India has to spend more US dollars -> This can pressure the Indian rupee to weaken (each rupee buys fewer dollars).
A weaker rupee and costlier crude oil make importing raw materials and manufacturing more expensive -> This can slowly push up domestic inflation (general rise in prices of goods and services).
Higher inflation and oil import costs can squeeze government finances and impact broader stock market sentiment, including sectors heavily reliant on energy.

impacts.rationale: Supply strains like the Iran war and Hormuz crisis keep global oil prices elevated, which is bad for everyday consumers as it makes energy costlier.
When oil prices rise, India needs more dollars to buy oil, weakening the rupee—making foreign travel and imported goods pricier for Indians.
Costlier crude translates to higher transport and production costs locally, leading to higher everyday prices—generally bad for household budgets.

watch_next: Updates on OPEC+ production quotas and Middle East supply routes
Movements in global crude oil benchmarks like Brent
analysis.caveats: Only the article text and headline were evaluated, and sudden diplomatic resolutions in the Middle East could quickly reverse global oil price spikes.

events.headline: RBI brings more gold home, shifts 165 tonnes from overseas vaults

items.title: RBI brings more gold home, shifts 165 tonnes from overseas vaults
items.summary: Between September 2025 and September 2026, the Reserve Bank of India increased its domestic gold holdings significantly. The domestic share of gold rose from 65.4% to 84%, while holdings in international banks decreased. Total gold holdings changed minimally, increasing from 880.18 tonnes to 880.52 tonnes. The share of gold in foreign exchange reserves fluctuated during this period due to price changes.

items.title: In gold we trust: Why is India turning its back on foreign vaults?
items.summary: India has sharply increased the share of its gold reserves held at home, with the RBI storing 740.13 tonnes domestically by September 2026, or 84% of its total holdings, after repatriating another 60.08 tonnes in six months. While the RBI says the move is operational, the freezing of Russian reserves has heightened global concerns over where sovereign assets are held, making domestic custody of gold increasingly attractive as a form of insurance.

items.title: Why is RBI bringing its gold back to India? The big shift decoded

events.article_text:
Between September 2025 and September 2026, the Reserve Bank of India increased its domestic gold holdings significantly. The domestic share of gold rose from 65.4% to 84%, while holdings in international banks decreased. Total gold holdings changed minimally, increasing from 880.18 tonnes to 880.52 tonnes. The share of gold in foreign exchange reserves fluctuated during this period due to price changes.

analysis.tldr: Moving gold back to Indian soil makes our national savings safer from foreign political risks, keeping the country's financial foundation secure.
the_story: Between September 2025 and September 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI [India's central bank that manages money and interest rates]) shifted 165 tonnes of gold from overseas vaults back to domestic storage.
The share of India's gold stored inside the country rose from 65.4% to 84%, reducing the amount kept in international banks.
Total gold holdings stayed almost the same, moving only slightly from 880.18 tonnes to 880.52 tonnes.
The overall share of gold in India's foreign exchange reserves (money kept in foreign currencies and gold to pay for imports) changed during this period due to shifting gold prices.
analysis.what_happened: The Reserve Bank of India brought a massive amount of its gold home from foreign countries between September 2025 and September 2026. Instead of keeping most of its precious metal safely locked up abroad like in UK vaults, the central bank decided to store 84% of it right inside India. This shift was done to protect India's wealth from overseas risks, while the actual amount of gold owned barely changed.
analysis.analogy: It is like moving your gold jewelry from a locker in a faraway city's bank back into your own home safe, so you can keep an eye on it yourself.
why_it_matters_india: The RBI shifts 165 tonnes of gold from foreign vaults to domestic storage.
India's gold is now physically within local borders, reducing dependence on foreign security.
Foreign exchange reserves remain secure and diversified against global political tensions.
Confidence in India's sovereign financial management stays high among citizens and global markets.

impacts.target: India's foreign exchange reserves (total money and gold held abroad)
impacts.rationale: Reserves held abroad decrease because the physical gold is being relocated home, though total national wealth remains unchanged — neutral for everyday people.
Relocating existing gold does not change global supply, but higher local security costs could slightly influence domestic premiums — generally making retail gold purchase pricier.

watch_next: Future announcements from the RBI on whether the remaining foreign gold will also be brought home
Global geopolitical trends affecting where countries choose to store their wealth
analysis.caveats: The article text is brief and combines the gold report with promotional website text, leaving out specific geopolitical reasons cited behind the vault shift.

events.headline: Russia, India, and Saudi Arabia Are Stalling a Key U.N. Climate Report

items.title: Russia, India, and Saudi Arabia Are Stalling a Key U.N. Climate Report
items.summary: Experts are warning that political attacks on a critical scientific report could undermine the basis for future U.N. climate negotiations. Read more on E360 →

events.article_text:
This article was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

Experts are warning that political attacks on a critical scientific report could undermine the basis for future U.N. climate negotiations.

The science that guides negotiators and policymakers at the United Nations’ COP31 climate change conference is “under a serious and highly politicized attack,” said Laurence Tubiana, a veteran French climate diplomat and one of the architects of the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, established in 1988 to inform international climate negotiations, regularly assesses thousands of studies on rising temperatures, sea level rise, melting ice, and strategies for adapting to the increasingly intense impacts of global warming.

But three countries — Russia and Saudi Arabia, both major fossil fuel producers, and India, which accounts for an estimated 14 percent of global coal consumption — are blocking progress on future reports, according to scientists on the panel and independent observers.

Those countries “are doing everything they can to slow the process,” Tubiana said. They are becoming less discreet about their efforts, she said, as they increasingly view their economies as threatened by a conditional agreement to transition away from coal, oil, and gas reached during COP28, the 2023 Conference of the Parties in Dubai.

The science panel’s current impasse is especially troubling, “because we know climate problems are accelerating, and we need a lot of data and communication to understand what’s happening at this COP,” said Mary Robinson, former president of Ireland and former United Nations special envoy on climate change.

Robinson said this isn’t the first time countries have tried to obstruct science. Recent examples include attacks seeking to undermine a recent United Nations Environment Programme report on “overshoot,” which concludes that there is no way to avoid passing the 1.5 degree C warming target in the Paris Agreement.

Fossil fuels account for an estimated 80 percent to 90 percent of planet-heating carbon dioxide emissions, according to the IPCC’s 2023 assessment.

The international climate science panel relies on voluntary donations from member countries to fund its work, including periodic assessments, some of which inform steps required under the Paris Agreement. The panel has yet to set a budget for next year, potentially delaying a scientific report needed ahead of next year’s U.N. climate conference.

“Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the oil and gas sector has become much more aggressive,” Tubiana said. “I think this is partly because it sees its dominance over energy starting to erode.”

Oil and gas companies are losing ground in transport as electric-vehicle adoption in Asia surges faster than expected, she said, adding that reports from the International Energy Agency show demand for fossil fuels is set to slow.

“Investors hear the message that the decline is coming, and those governments have pushed back,” she said.

The 2023 IPCC report concluded that existing and planned fossil fuel infrastructure would push global warming beyond the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming as close as possible to 1.5 degrees C above the preindustrial average.

Tubiana said a growing number of countries view the transition away from fossil fuels as a path to greater energy independence and security, while those opposed to the shift are becoming “more angry and vocal.”

“The danger,” she said, “is that they take other countries along with them that aren’t necessarily committed to that position.”

The latest draft of the conference’s decision document highlights the assessments’ importance to the negotiations. Some countries also want to include language that could help break the science panel’s deadlock, but the same countries stalling the IPCC are resisting that effort.

In particular, the climate, environment, and energy ministers participating in the current round of talks could help the IPCC get over the political hurdles it faces, said Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute.

Hare said the countries participating in the U.N. talks should advocate for continued support for the IPCC. If the panel can’t deliver the needed climate science “because of political obstacles created by a small number of countries, it would be a historic setback for the connection between science and the international climate process.”

Robinson said some of the world’s least developed countries and small island states “desperately need” the international panel’s reports because they can’t do their own climate assessments.

“We need the authoritative, legitimate IPCC science, which has guided us from the beginning in this whole climate process,” she said. “It’s just a sign of the difficult times we’re in that we have to fight for it. I can hardly believe it.”

analysis.tldr: Political friction over climate reports could eventually alter how global funds and rules target Indian energy and coal companies.
the_story: Russia, Saudi Arabia, and India (which accounts for an estimated 14 percent of global coal consumption) are blocking progress on future U.N. climate science reports.
Experts say these countries view their economies as threatened by the 2023 COP28 agreement to transition away from coal, oil, and gas.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (established in 1988 to inform climate negotiations) relies on voluntary donations and has yet to set a budget for next year, threatening delays.
analysis.what_happened: India, along with Russia and Saudi Arabia, is stalling a key U.N. climate science report process. This is happening because these nations fear that transitioning away from fossil fuels—as agreed at the 2023 COP28 conference—threatens their domestic economic interests.
analysis.analogy: It is like a group of students trying to stall a final textbook being printed because they worry the test questions inside will make their preferred study methods look bad.
why_it_matters_india: India relies heavily on coal (accounting for 14 percent of global consumption) to power its economy.
Governments push back against climate panels because global investors are hearing that fossil fuel demand will slow down.
Stalling international climate reports delays the pressure to rapidly phase out traditional energy sources.
This political standoff shapes future international funding rules and green energy expectations for Indian firms.

impacts.target: Indian coal & fossil fuel companies (like Coal India)
impacts.rationale: Slowing down international climate reports and defending fossil fuel usage keeps near-term demand for domestic coal stable, which can be seen as good for traditional energy businesses.

impacts.target: Green energy & renewable stocks in India (solar/EV firms)
impacts.rationale: When governments push back against global climate transitions, it can create mixed signals for long-term clean energy funding enthusiasm.

watch_next: Whether the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change manages to secure its budget for next year
Updates from upcoming U.N. climate change conferences regarding transition rules
analysis.caveats: The article focuses on international political negotiations, so the direct impact on everyday consumer prices or retail stocks remains indirect and slow-moving.

analysis.tldr: A panel discussion by foreign policy experts warns that global oil supplies face risks due to security crises in a vital shipping lane, which could eventually make fuel costlier for you.
the_story: A panel discussion hosted by Vijay V. Vaitheeswaran at the Council on Foreign Relations explored the uncertain future of U.S. security guarantees for the free flow of oil.
The panelists discussed the ongoing crisis in the Strait of Hormuz (a narrow sea passage crucial for global oil shipments) and its effects on energy security.
The guest experts included Edward L. Morse from Hartree Partners, Kelly Sims Gallagher from The Fletcher School, and Kevin Book from ClearView Energy Partners.
analysis.what_happened: Experts gathered for a panel discussion to debate how safe the global oil supply really is right now, specifically focusing on the Strait of Hormuz. Because the provided article is just a short announcement and summary of the event rather than a news report of a specific new event, details of any actual physical disruption are not mentioned.
analysis.analogy: It is like living in a gated community where everyone relies on one security guard at the main gate, but neighbors start arguing about whether that guard will keep watching the gate tomorrow.
why_it_matters_india: Any security crisis in major oil-shipping lanes raises fears about future oil supplies.
Global oil prices tend to jump when traders worry about oil shipments getting blocked.
Since India imports most of its crude oil, costlier global oil increases import bills.
A higher oil import bill puts pressure on the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars) and pushes up domestic inflation (general rise in prices).

impacts.rationale: Fears over shipping lanes and oil security typically push oil prices higher, which is bad for everyday consumers because it leads to pricier petrol and diesel.
When crude oil gets more expensive, India needs more dollars to buy it, which weakens the rupee — making imported goods costlier for everyone.
Higher oil prices increase transport and manufacturing costs across the board, driving up prices of everyday goods and hurting household budgets.

watch_next: Actual security developments or shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz
Official statements on U.S. energy security policies or military posture in the Middle East
analysis.caveats: The article text is a short promotional event description rather than a breaking news report, so it discusses potential risks debated by experts rather than an actual physical disruption happening right now.

events.headline: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom

items.title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
items.summary: In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. events.article_text:
In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10. And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants. How did we get here?

If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today.

But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants.

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.

This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report. That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google (18%), Amazon (16%), and Microsoft (25%). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there.

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation.

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead.

It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source.

But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025.

There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about demand flexibility—efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high.

Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.

analysis.tldr: A massive surge in US electricity demand from AI data centers is driving up natural gas use, which can push global fuel import costs higher for energy-importing nations like India.
the_story: The data center boom for artificial intelligence is fueling a massive resurgence in natural gas power in the United States.
For example, plans for a Meta data center in Louisiana expanded its power needs, leading the local utility to increase planned natural-gas plants from three to 10.
PJM, the largest US power grid operator covering parts of 13 states, reported that nearly half of the 200 gigawatts of proposed power projects in its connection queue are natural-gas plants.
Due to soaring power demands, Meta's greenhouse-gas emissions jumped 45% over last year, while Google, Amazon, and Microsoft saw emissions increases of 18%, 16%, and 25% respectively.
Data center developers are increasingly planning to build over 100 off-grid on-site natural-gas power plants totaling 115 gigawatts to bypass long grid connection wait times.
analysis.what_happened: A massive surge in electricity demand from AI data centers in the United States is causing a boom in natural gas usage. Because renewable energy options like wind and solar face long wait times to connect to power grids, utility companies and tech firms are turning to natural gas power plants to get electricity running quickly.
analysis.analogy: It is like a whole neighborhood suddenly buying electric cars and overloading the local transformer, forcing everyone to set up noisy personal diesel generators in their yards just to keep the lights on.
why_it_matters_india: US data centers consume massive amounts of natural gas to power AI infrastructure.
This drives up global demand and competition for natural gas.
Higher global gas demand makes imported Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG [super-cooled natural gas transported by ships]) more expensive for countries like India.
Pricier imported gas increases input costs for Indian fertilizer plants, power generators, and city gas distribution companies, raising domestic inflation pressures.

impacts.target: Global LNG and natural gas prices
impacts.rationale: Increased US domestic consumption and off-grid gas generation projects tighten global supplies, making imported fuel costlier — bad for Indian energy importers.
Higher imported energy and fertilizer feedstock costs push up everyday consumer prices in India — bad for ordinary households.
Costlier energy imports mean India has to spend more US dollars to buy fuel, putting downward pressure on the local currency.

watch_next: Global liquefied natural gas shipping prices and trade data
Updates on major US power grid operator rules for natural gas hookups
analysis.caveats: If renewable energy technologies and battery storage scale up faster than expected, utility companies might rely less heavily on natural gas.

history.title: When the safest thing in finance turned out not to be
history.what: American house prices fell, mortgage securities that were rated as safe as government bonds proved worthless, and Lehman Brothers was allowed to fail. Global credit markets stopped functioning within days.
history.why: Mortgages were bundled into securities, sliced into tranches, and rated AAA on the assumption that house prices would never fall across the whole country at once. That assumption had held for decades, so it was treated as a law. Banks held these with very little of their own capital behind them, and insured each other through derivatives — which concentrated the risk rather than spreading it.
history.impact: Global shares fell more than 50%. World trade collapsed faster than in 1929. Unemployment doubled in the US and Europe. India's Sensex fell about 60% and the rupee slid sharply, despite Indian banks holding almost none of the toxic assets — a pure demonstration that a foreign-funded market imports foreign panic.
history.policy: Bank bailouts, then zero interest rates and quantitative easing — central banks creating money to buy bonds — on a scale never attempted before. Regulation followed: Basel III forced banks to hold far more capital, and Dodd-Frank restricted what they could trade with their own money.
history.consequence: Banks became safer and far less profitable, and much risky lending simply migrated to less-regulated non-bank lenders — where it still sits. A decade of near-zero rates inflated the price of every asset and widened wealth inequality sharply, which reshaped the politics of the following decade.
history.pattern: The dangerous asset is never the one everybody calls risky. It is the one everybody calls safe, because that is where leverage accumulates unexamined. Ask what today's "obviously safe" holding is, and what would have to be true for it not to be.
history.india_echo: India's own version arrived in 2018 when IL&FS, rated AAA, defaulted and froze the entire non-bank lending sector. Same shape: a AAA rating, heavy short-term borrowing funding long-term assets, and a regulator watching the wrong institution.
history.watch_for: Ratings doing the thinking for investors. When a security is bought because of its rating rather than its cash flows, the rating is the risk.
